articles.title: Ranking the NBA's Biggest Bag Fumbles of the Past 15 Years
articles.summary: Every offseason, dozens of NBA players cash in by signing contracts for life-changing amounts of money. Not every player is so fortunate, though. When the…
articles.body:
Every offseason, dozens of NBA players cash in by signing contracts for life-changing amounts of money.

Not every player is so fortunate, though. When the free-agent game of musical chairs ends and cap space dries up around the league, plenty of players are forced to sign below-market deals and try their luck again next year.

Here, we're focused on the players who blew the biggest bags in recent years.

Players who lost out on major paydays because of injuries won't be appearing in these rankings. Victor Oladipo, DeMarcus Cousins and Isaiah Thomas all made far less money than they would have prior to their respective career-altering injuries, but that isn't their fault.

The players featured here all had a choice at some point. They all just chose poorly from a financial standpoint.

We've ranked them here based on how much they reportedly gave up, what they ended up signing for and how much each of them earned from that point forward.

Heading into the 2024 offseason, the Miami Heat offered Caleb Martin a five-year, $65 million extension, according to Ira Winderman of the South Florida Sun Sentinel. He would have needed to pick up his $7.1 million player option in 2024-25, and the Heat would have tacked on an extra four years and $58 million from there.

Instead, Martin declined his player option to become an unrestricted free agent. He wound up signing a four-year, $35 million deal with the Philadelphia 76ers that contained an additional $5.3 million in unlikely-to-be-earned incentives.

"I mean, you're always going to wish you can make as much money as you can," Martin told reporters after he signed with the Sixers. "It's part of the game, it's part of life. You live and learn. You take risks. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't."

Martin didn't even last a full season with the Sixers. They sent him to the Dallas Mavericks ahead of the 2025 trade deadline for Quentin Grimes, and it's been all downhill for him ever since. In 2025-26, he averaged a career-low 3.9 points in 14.8 minutes per game.

Martin is earning $10.0 million in 2026-27 and has a $9.4 million player option in 2027-28, which will be his age-32 campaign. In theory, he'll still have a chance to recoup some of the money he lost by declining the Heat's offer in 2024. But barring a drastic turnaround, it's difficult to imagine him receiving an offer that tops his player option in 2027.

Martin might be a minimum or near-minimum player from here on out, which means this could wind up being a roughly $30 million bag fumble.

Jonathan Kuminga and the Golden State Warriors spent the entire 2025 offseason in a restricted-free-agency standoff. Shortly before the Oct. 1 qualifying-offer deadline, Kuminga agreed to sign a two-year, $46.8 million deal with a second-year team option.

The deal was "designed for the Warriors—or another team if and when Kuminga is traded during the upcoming season—to rip up and complete a fresh new contract after the 2025-26 campaign," ESPN's Shams Charania reported at the time . The Warriors did trade Kuminga to the Atlanta Hawks ahead of the trade deadline, and the Hawks did decline their $24.3 million team option on Kuminga, but that's just about all that went according to plan for him.

Instead of landing a hefty payday, Kuminga once again languished in free agency for nearly two months. Finally, in late August, he agreed to sign a two-year, $12.4 million contract with the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Kuminga did secure a second-year player option, so he'll have another chance to cash in as a free agent in 2027. But he's earning less than $6.1 million in 2026-27, which is a far cry from the team option that the Hawks declined.

Here's where it gets painful: The Warriors reportedly offered Kuminga two contract structures during their standoff in 2025. They offered him the two-year, $46.8 million deal that he wound up signing, and a three-year, $75 million contract with a third-year team option, according to Charania and ESPN's Anthony Slater .

In essence, Kuminga could have been guaranteed $24.3 million in 2026-27, and the Warriors would have had a $26.1 million team option on him in 2027-28. Instead, he's now set to earn roughly $18.2 million less in 2026-27, but he'll have the freedom to become an unrestricted free agent in 2027.

The jury is still out on how momentous of a bag fumble this winds up being, but for now, Kuminga's agent has a lot of explaining to do.

In 2016, the Brooklyn Nets signed restricted free agent Donatas Motiejūnas to a four-year, $37 million offer sheet, according to ESPN's Calvin Watkins . The Houston Rockets decided to match, which is where the drama typically ends for restricted free agents.

Motiejūnas proved to be the exception to that rule.

According to Watkins , the Rockets only had to match the "principal terms" of the offer sheet, which was $31 million. As a result, Motiejūnas then refused to show up for his physical, leaving the Rockets to wait him out or pull the offer sheet and let him become a restricted free agent again.

The Rockets initially did the latter, but they then signed Motiejūnas to a four-year, $35 million deal . However, an issue arose in his physical, and the Rockets wound up renouncing their rights to him entirely. That made him an unrestricted free agent who was free to sign with any team.

Motiejūnas wound up signing a one-year, $1.5 million minimum-salary contract with the New Orleans Pelicans. He played only 37 NBA games in total from that point forward.

That's a casual $35-plus million bag fumble.

Michael Jordan expected to leave media role

After the NBA's salary cap exploded in 2016, the Minnesota Timberwolves offered Shabazz Muhammad a four-year extension "believed to be worth at least $40 million," according to Jerry Zgoda of the Star Tribune .

The following summer, he wound up re-signing with the Timberwolves on a two-year, $3.4 million minimum-salary contract.

According to ESPN's Adrian Wojnarowski , "Muhammad re-signed with the Timberwolves last offseason with hopes of a substantial bench role, only to find [then-head coach Tom] Thibodeau reverting to the longstanding practices of shorter bench rotations and heavy starter minutes that became a staple of his five years as Chicago Bulls coach." He averaged only 9.7 minutes per game with Minnesota in 2017-18 after playing 20.5 minutes per game over the previous three seasons.

Muhammad asked for the Timberwolves to either send him elsewhere at the 2018 trade deadline or release him, according to Wojnarowski. They eventually chose the latter, leading him to sign a rest-of-season contract with the Milwaukee Bucks. Muhammad played in 11 games for the Bucks that season and has yet to appear in an NBA game since then.

Muhammad met with the Los Angeles Lakers when he was a free agent and reportedly turned down bigger offers from other teams to re-sign with the Timberwolves, per Zgoda. Considering how caustically their partnership ended later that season, it might have been better for both parties to part ways in free agency.

Montrezl Harrell hit free agency at the perfect time in 2020. He was fresh off winning the NBA's Sixth Man of the Year award after averaging a career-high 18.6 points and 7.1 rebounds per game while shooting 58.0 percent overall with the Los Angeles Clippers.

Harrell just finished a two-year, $12 million contract with the Clippers and appeared poised for a significant raise. He wound up signing a two-year, $19.0 million deal with the Los Angeles Lakers and never got more than a minimum contract after that.

Brad Turner of the Los Angeles Times reported that Harrell turned down a bigger offer from the Charlotte Hornets when he signed with the Lakers. According to ESPN's Kendrick Perkins , the Hornets offered him a four-year, $80 million deal.

Considering that Harrell earned roughly $25 million over that same span, this would be a legendary bag fumble if Perkins is right. Harrell earned nearly $39.5 million across his nine-year career.

If Harrell won a championship with the Lakers, perhaps the discount would have been worth it. He was joining the reigning champions, after all. The only problem is, they lost in the first round of the playoffs in 2020-21 and missed the playoffs entirely the following season.

In February 2021, the Los Angeles Lakers approached Dennis Schröder's agent to discuss a contract extension, according to ESPN's Dave McMenamin . They reportedly offered him a four-year, $84 million deal, per ESPN's Brian Windhorst (via Dan Feldman of NBC Sports), but McMenamin reported that "Schröder's side said they would rather wait until the offseason to discuss a deal when he reached free agency."

Although Schröder averaged 15.4 points, 5.8 assists and 3.5 rebounds per game for the Lakers during the 2020-21 season, the free-agent market wasn't kind to him the following summer. He wound up settling for a one-year, $5.9 million contract with the Boston Celtics via the taxpayer mid-level exception.

Schröder initially had a good sense of humor about his bag fumble. However, he later began pushing back on the narrative that he turned down an extension offer from the Lakers.

"I mean, end of the day, there never was a contract," Schröder told McMenamin. "There never was a contract, never rejected anything ... That's not true."

Had the Lakers made him an official offer, Schröder told Jake Fischer of Yahoo Sports that he would have signed it. "I would never just leave money on the table," he added. "My mom didn't raise me that way."

In 2022, Schröder took a one-year, $2.7 million contract to rejoin the Lakers. And he finally did cash in by signing a two-year, $25.4 million contract with the Toronto Raptors in 2023 and a three-year, $44.3 million deal with the Detroit Pistons two years later.

Still, the roughly $34 million he earned over that four-season stretch pales in comparison to the $84 million deal that the Lakers were reportedly willing to offer him in 2021.

When Nerlens Noel entered restricted free agency in 2017, the Dallas Mavericks offered him a four-year, $70 million deal, according to ESPN's Tim MacMahon . Noel declined and requested a max contract, at which point the Mavericks "immediately pulled the offer off the table and never made another one," per MacMahon.

Noel wound up signing his $4.2 million qualifying offer with the Mavericks instead. The following summer, he left Dallas to sign a two-year, $3.8 million minimum-salary contract with the Oklahoma City Thunder.

From there, Noel signed a one-year, $5 million deal with the New York Knicks in 2020 and then re-upped on a three-year, $28.8 million contract the following summer. However, he wound up getting bought out of that contract in February 2023 and has appeared in only three NBA games since then.

In total, he came nowhere close to recouping what the Mavericks originally offered to pay him in 2017.

"They think he should of taken the [$17 million]," a source close to the Mavericks told SB Nation's Tim Cato at the time. "That's a good number for him. But if he's willing to risk it and bet on himself, you can't knock someone looking for their first big bag of money."

Noel wound up suing his former agent, Rich Paul of Klutch Sports, after Klutch accused Noel of not paying his commission on one of his contracts, according to Windhorst . A judge dismissed his lawsuit in September 2022, and the two sides settled a few months later .

Everyone featured here so far turned down tens of millions of dollars. James Harden is the only one who's turned down hundreds of millions.

In 2021, the Brooklyn Nets offered Harden a three-year, $161 million contract extension, according to Brian Lewis of the New York Post . Harden declined to sign it, perhaps in part because he would be eligible for a four-year, $227 million extension the ensuing offseason.

Five months later, the Nets traded him to the Philadelphia 76ers, where he reunited with former Houston Rockets team president Daryl Morey.

That reunion proved fruitful at first. Morey convinced Harden to sign a two-year, $68.6 million below-max contract, which gave the Sixers enough space under the first apron to use both the non-taxpayer MLE to sign P.J. Tucker and the bi-annual exception to sign Danuel House Jr. Harden got a second-year player option on the deal, which allowed him to opt out and try to cash in the following summer if he wanted.

Things went south between Harden and the Sixers ahead of his opt-in decision in 2023. Morey and the Sixers reportedly ghosted Harden in the days leading up to the start of free agency, which eventually led him to pick up his option and request a trade.

That was not exactly the $227 million payday that was promised.

The Sixers eventually traded Harden to the Los Angeles Clippers last fall, but the NBA's new collective bargaining agreement effectively defanged the unmatched spending power of team governor Steve Ballmer. With the second apron looming large, the Clippers refused to give Harden or Kawhi Leonard full max contracts. Instead, Harden agreed to a two-year, $70 million deal with a second-year player option.

In total, Harden made just over $100 million across the three seasons that his extension with the Nets would have spanned. Granted, he's now one of the only players in NBA history with more than $500 million in career earnings , so he'll be fine either way.

Still, misreading the market for mid-30s stars in the new CBA landscape cost Harden upward of $60 million.

Unless otherwise noted, all stats via NBA.com , PBPStats , Cleaning the Glass or Basketball Reference . All salary information via Spotrac and salary-cap information via RealGM .

articles.title: Why is Michael Jordan bidding farewell to his lucrative $40 million-a-year deal? All about the NBA upset
articles.summary: NBA News: There will not be any debate around the fact that the end of Michael Jordan’s NBC role as an analyst is going to be a major upset for the fans worldwi.
articles.body: There will not be any debate around the fact that the end of Michael Jordan’s NBC role as an analyst is going to be a major upset for the fans worldwide. Regardless, MJ is reportedly not coming back to the role. While the contract was quite lucrative with a whopping $40 million a year attached to the deal, we all need to question, does Jordan need more money? For context, Jordan is the wealthiest athlete in the world with over a staggering $4.3 billion net worth to his name, according to Forbes. But what’s actually going on and what’s the real reason behind Jordan’s reported decision.Why Michael Jordan won't return for NBC's $40 million NBA dealMichael Jordan appears to be done with NBC. Multiple reports this week point to the NBA legend skipping a second season with the network, ending a run that once looked like the year's biggest broadcasting coup.The move comes after Jordan signed on last year for a reported $40 million a year as a special contributor to NBC's NBA coverage. What changed between that splashy announcement and now is a story of high expectations, thin output, and a legend who has never liked talking much anyway.Michael Jordan reportedly not returning to NBC's NBA coverageAccording to Front Office Sports, Jordan is unlikely to be part of NBC's basketball coverage for the 2026-27 season. The Daily Mail reached out to NBC for comment and did not hear back.Jordan's addition to the network last May was billed as a coup, since he had barely appeared on camera since The Last Dance aired in 2020. Fans expected regular appearances and sharp analysis throughout the season. Instead, Jordan sat down with host Mike Tirico just once. The single conversation got split into five segments and rolled out across several weeks of the campaign, which left part of the audience unimpressed.Some fans and analysts felt shortchanged. They wanted more from a name as big as Jordan's, and five scattered clips over months did not match the buildup.Why Michael Jordan is not coming back to NBCTirico pushed back hard against the criticism. He pointed out that Jordan has never been much of a talker, and noted Jordan's ownership stake in the Charlotte Hornets and his role at Jordan Brand as reasons his time is stretched thin. According to Tirico, Jordan wanted to focus specifically on where he sees the state of the league right now, not run through a long list of topics.Jordan reportedly used part of that conversation to question whether today's highest paid stars love the game as much as his generation did. Tirico defended the format anyway: "Was it better than not hearing from Michael Jordan? You're damn right it was."He added that hearing Jordan's take as the greatest player of all time carries a weight that a hundred hot takes about a single injury never will.Backlash puts NBC's marquee hire in questionNot everyone bought the defense. Charles Barkley, never shy with an opinion, put it plainly: "It's a bad look for NBC." The comment stuck, and it captured a frustration that had been building since the deal was first announced.Front Office Sports did not report an official reason behind the expected exit. That silence leaves room for speculation about whether the split was Jordan's call, the network's, or something both sides worked out quietly and would rather not detail.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Osetkowski: ""La identidad de Valencia encaja muy bien en mi juego"
articles.standfirst: El ala-pívot, radiante durante su presentación como nuevo jugador taronja
articles.summary: El ala-pívot, radiante durante su presentación como nuevo jugador taronja
articles.body: El interior americano con pasaporte alemán, Dylan Osetkowski, valoró este jueves su incorporación al Valencia Basket y destacó que la idea de juego del conjunto 'taronja' fue uno de los principales argumentos para incorporarse al equipo. "Estoy muy cómodo jugando en España por el ritmo de juego que hay en los partidos y la identidad de Valencia Basket encaja muy bien en mi juego. Es un ritmo rápido y fuerte", explicó Osetkowski en declaraciones a los medios de comunicación durante su presentación como nuevo jugador del Valencia Basket. Sobre su objetivo individual, Osetkowski se centró en ganar el máximo número de partidos: "Es un año histórico después de la pasada temporada con los títulos y ahora con el 40 aniversario. Estoy aquí para ayudar al club y para ganar, no para anotar y buscar los máximos puntos". El nuevo jugador 'taronja' también habló sobre sus primeros días en el club y sobre sus conversaciones con el entrenador Xavi Albert: "Me ha pedido que dé el máximo y que ayude tanto en la posición de cuatro como de cinco. Voy a centrarme en ello y en cumplir con las expectativas". Osetkowski se reencuentra esta temporada con Kameron Taylor, Mario Saint-Supéry y Yankuba Sima, quienes fueron compañeros en Unicaja de Málaga, y definió esta situación como "única". "Me han ayudado a conocer las normas, la identidad y a encajar rápido. También noto una comunión muy fuerte desde el principio". Víctor Luengo, director de relaciones externas del conjunto 'taronja', también valoró la incorporación de Osetkowski: "Es un jugador versátil que nos puede ayudar en las dos posiciones interiores. Llega en un momento de madurez y de experiencia al máximo nivel que serán muy beneficiosas para el equipo. Nos gusta mucho de él que es consistente y sólido y que no necesita ser protagonista".

articles.title: Kevin Durant Hypes 'Juggernaut' 76ers After LeBron James, Jaylen Brown Join Loaded Roster
articles.summary: Add Kevin Durant to the list of people eager to see what the new-look Philadelphia 76ers can do this season.
articles.body:
Add Kevin Durant to the list of people eager to see what the new-look Philadelphia 76ers can do this season.

Appearing on the Boardroom Talks show with Speedy Morman (starts at 12:15 mark), Durant said the Sixers are going to be a "juggernaut" with LeBron James and Jaylen Brown joining a roster that already has Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid and VJ Edgecombe.

The 76ers were undeniably among the biggest winners of the NBA offseason. They entered the summer seemingly bogged down in part by Paul George's contract, which has $110.7 million remaining over two years if he exercises his player option for 2027-28.

George's deal had been regarded as one of the worst in the NBA during the 2025-26 season, yet the Sixers were able to offload it in a trade that brought back Brown after he finished sixth in MVP voting.

The Brown trade was followed up with James signing a two-year, $8 million contract to join him in Philadelphia.

There are still a lot of questions about how the Sixers' on-court operation is going to look with Brown, James, Maxey and Embiid all needing to have the ball to maximize their abilities.

Head coach Nick Nurse will be tasked with figuring all of that out. It also remains to be seen if Embiid can remain healthy to make it through a full season and playoffs.

Even with all of those potential concerns, the upside for this group is as high as it has been for any 76ers team in recent memory.

Durant will get to see what this group looks like in person on Nov. 28 when the Houston Rockets host the Sixers at the Toyota Center. They will meet again in Philadelphia on Dec. 23.

articles.title: Kevin Durant Talks Russell Westbrook's 'Shocking' NBA Retirement, 'I Thought He Could Still Play'
articles.summary: Kevin Durant will forever be connected to Russell Westbrook after they starred together for the Oklahoma City Thunder early in their legendary careers, and he called it "shocking" that his former teammate retired this offseason.
articles.body:
Kevin Durant will forever be connected to Russell Westbrook after they starred together for the Oklahoma City Thunder early in their legendary careers, and he called it "shocking" that his former teammate retired this offseason.

"It just hit me, man, that's one of the first dudes you come in with and you were around every day to finally step out," Durant said on an episode of Boardroom Talks (10:15 mark). "A lot of guys that have been younger than me or drafted after me have retired, but I wasn't as close to them as I was to Russell. And it's somebody I feel like could still play. It surprised me. It's one of those things that you can appreciate all the time spent, and somebody like Russell is doing a lot off the court too. I want to see what he does next.

"... It was shocking. Like I said, I thought he could still play. I feel like he would have been a good veteran presence in the locker room."

Had Westbrook wanted to remain in the NBA, he could have for the 2026-27 campaign.

After all, he reportedly had offers from the Washington Wizards and Sacramento Kings but decided he instead wanted to retire.

Durant and Westbrook essentially ushered the Oklahoma City Thunder into basketball relevance as a franchise together. The former played his rookie season with the Seattle SuperSonics and then went to OKC with the franchise for his second season.

That second season just so happened to be Westbrook's rookie year.

It didn't take long for them to find success, as the Thunder reached the Western Conference Finals four times and the NBA Finals once during their eight seasons as teammates. While they never quite got over the hump to win a title, they were consistently among the league's best.

Durant eventually left for the Golden State Warriors and won both of his championships alongside Stephen Curry. And in the aftermath of that move, his relationship with Westbrook was publicly scrutinized and drew plenty of attention.

But the future Hall of Famer had nothing but respect and admiration for Westbrook in his latest comments as he reflected on the guard's retirement and their time together.

articles.title: When it comes to Air Jordans, Michael Jordan is still calling the shots
articles.summary: At 63, the six-time champion remains deeply involved in the design of the Air Jordan 41.
articles.body:
At 63 years old, Michael Jordan remains incredibly active, driven, competitive and detail-oriented.

He co-owns NASCAR's 23XI Racing, whose driver Tyler Reddick became the first competitor to win the first three races of a season earlier this year. Reddick is a contender for the team's first championship, and we know how much MJ is obsessed with those. "I'm entrenched in the sport as a whole," he told CBS' Gayle King earlier this year.

So it should come as no surprise that Jordan remains actively involved in the design and creative process of the eponymous Air Jordan brand that helped make him a billionaire off the court, and propelled the sneaker industry to global popularity in the ensuing decades. The Air Jordan 41 design was released on Thursday, with the product first available starting on Friday in China prior to a global release. And Michael Jordan's input is still vital to the Nike executives charged with bringing the shoe to life, from initial briefings to the final sign-off approval.

"He's our competitive advantage to everybody in the industry," Donald Kelsey, Jordan Brand's senior director of basketball and promo footwear, told reporters earlier this month. "If you think about his access to what he sees, it's like the top 1%. Whether that's watches, automobiles, aircrafts. What he sees in the world of innovation and technology, he's already like five, 10 years ahead. He's not playing anymore, but he's involved throughout the entire process."

When Kelsey and Leo Chang, Jordan Brand's creative director of basketball and sport, met with Jordan several times over the last year in creating the AJ41, Jordan was giving them a litmus test on how they were pushing innovation. Whereas most basketball shoes are created for the offensive side of the ball — since almost all the hoops highlights we see are scoring, shooting and passing — the 41 was built to cater to defenders as well.

"When you talk to MJ, he has a plan to defend even the modern day players like he was still playing," Chang said. "That's how competitive he is. He talked a lot about the mentality of 'by the time you see me, it's too late.'"

Jordan, a nine-time NBA All-Defensive First-Team member and one of three players in league history to win MVP and defensive player of the year in the same season, discussed treating defense like offense and facilitating the necessary footwork to achieve that. Certain elements you see in the 41, including a carbon fiber center and a heel zoom airbag, were implemented in part because MJ wanted to emphasize defensive mobility and agility. Additionally, each colorway of the new shoe is modeled after a gemstone, to reflect MJ's mentality and personal symbolism.

"The Air Jordan 41 is a statement about where Jordan Brand is headed," said Sarah Mensah, Jordan Brand's president. "It carries forward a legacy built on greatness, but it was created for the athletes, whose culture and style of play are defining the future of the game. It is more than the next Air Jordan. It is a signal of the next chapter of Jordan performance."

Chang has had the opportunity to visit Jordan's personal garage, which he described as 10 times nicer than any car museum you've ever been to. The attention to detail that went into the several dozen supercars MJ owns helped influence the shoe and its design as well. MJ inspired the static vertical lines you see across the sides of the shoes because he wanted them to look like they're moving even while standing still.

In any NASCAR or Formula 1 car, every granular detail, every ounce of weight distributed throughout the vehicle, is intentional to maximize optimal performance. It's clear that Jordan's 23XI NASCAR ownership has seeped into how he sees sneaker design.

"He's able to see how they are engineering and designing performance to meet the new regulations and performance standards that each car has," Kelsey told me. "So he's looking at that innovation and trying to apply it to how we approach our new technology."

Whether on the court or in the boardroom, Michael Jordan can give off an intimidating presence. He's not someone you want to cross or be on his bad side, because he's become a master of his craft in both basketball and footwear over the past 40-plus years who does not mess around.

"You have to show up dialed in and know what you're talking about, because otherwise he will call you out on it," Chang said. "He's seen it and heard it all. He's had some of the best designers on his stuff, so you can't really pull anything on him. He's still the best in the game in terms of having a conversation about product."

Every sample prototype Chang, Kelsey and the Jordan Brand designs is also produced in MJ's size 13. He tried on different versions of the 41 with and without various elements, finally coming around on the low-top iteration that a lot of today's elite athletes prefer. The Jordan Brand team talks to male and female pro, college and prep athletes across the world to discuss their preferences and what they're looking for to play at their very best. Kelsey and the team then relay that information to Jordan, to compare notes on what they're seeing and what he's seeing.

"Then we iron it out from there," Kelsey said, "but I wouldn't say there's any tension. For him, he's very keen and sharp. His archive is crazy, so it's just taking that information and making sure that as we go through this process, we're pushing it forward with a mix of innovation and expression."

The process for building the Air Jordan 42s has already begun, and Jordan is actively involved in the early stages with rough samples. The design and production team tries to maximize every chance they get to meet with him in person for any kind of insight. Because after 41 years of shoe design, all-time greatness on the court, and decades of ownership experience in both the NBA and NASCAR, his competitive energy and detail-oriented nature still burns bright. And for the signature product bearing his name, Michael Jordan is still very much deeply embedded in the game.

articles.title: Tavares prioriza el Madrid y renuncia a Cabo Verde para cuidar su rodilla
articles.standfirst: El gigante no arriesga su salud y se baja de las Ventanas FIBA para ponerse a punto físicamente con el club blanco
articles.summary: El gigante no arriesga su salud y se baja de las Ventanas FIBA para ponerse a punto físicamente con el club blanco
articles.body: Edy Tavares ha decidido priorizar al Real Madrid y su recuperación. El pívot caboverdiano, incluido inicialmente en la convocatoria de su selección para afrontar las Ventanas FIBA ante Túnez, Guinea y Nigeria, finalmente no viajará con Cabo Verde. El objetivo es claro: seguir con su preparación de cara a la próxima temporada y cuidar su estado físico después de un curso marcado por las lesiones. La decisión llega especialmente después de la lesión de rodilla izquierda que le dejó fuera del tramo final de la pasada temporada. Tavares, que ha estado cuatro meses apartado de las pistas, considera que ahora lo más importante es completar su recuperación sin asumir riesgos innecesarios. "Después de pensarlo mucho, he decidido no participar en esta convocatoria con la Selección de Cabo Verde", escribió en sus redes sociales. El madridista explica los motivos de su renuncia y pone por delante la prudencia. "Tras cuatro meses fuera por las lesiones, creo que lo más responsable es quedarme con mi equipo, seguir recuperándome y volver poco a poco". Una decisión que encaja con la prioridad del Real Madrid: que su jugador franquicia en la pintura llegue en las mejores condiciones posibles al inicio de una temporada especialmente exigente. Tavares no olvida aún así el compromiso que considera inquebrantable con su país. "Representar a Cabo Verde siempre será un orgullo. Esta vez toca dar un paso atrás para volver más fuerte". Cabo Verde afronta estas Ventanas con un balance de 3-3, en la sexta posición de su grupo, y obligado a pelear por una de las plazas que dan acceso al Mundial de 2027. El gigante quiso cerrar su mensaje dejando claro que su ausencia es temporal: "No es un adiós. Es un hasta pronto. Volveré. Más fuerte. Más preparado". Mientras Tavares se centra en el Real Madrid, Pedro Martínez tiene hasta siete jugadores movilizados con sus selecciones en estas Ventanas FIBA: Facu Campazzo y Gabriel Deck con Argentina, Timothé Luwawu-Cabarrot con Francia, Andrés Feliz con República Dominicana, Gabriele Procida con Italia, Mikael Jantunen con Finlandia y Jaime Pradilla con España.

articles.title: Los jugadores de la NBA exigen su parte del negocio de la NBA Europa: "Tenemos un problema muy serio"
articles.standfirst: El sindicato de jugadores de la NBA quiere su trozo del pastel europeo, considera inadmisible quedar al margen de esa operación y lo reclamará en la negociación del Convenio Colectivo
articles.summary: El sindicato de jugadores de la NBA quiere su trozo del pastel europeo, considera inadmisible quedar al margen de esa operación y lo reclamará en la negociación del Convenio Colectivo
articles.body: David Kelly, nuevo director ejecutivo de la NBPA, la poderosa Asociación de Jugadores de la NBA, ha lanzado un aviso contundente sobre el proyecto NBA Europa, previsto para comenzar en otoño de 2027, en una entrevista con Front Office Sports. Kelly dibuja una NBPA mucho más combativa ante el nacimiento de NBA Europa. No cuestiona que la NBA quiera expandirse en Europa, sino que considera que los jugadores de la NBA no pueden quedar al margen del negocio que se construya sobre el valor que ellos mismos han generado. Y adelanta que esa será una de las cuestiones importantes cuando llegue la próxima negociación del convenio colectivo. La posición del sindicato es que los jugadores actuales y los que han pasado por la NBA han contribuido decisivamente a construir el valor, la imagen y el prestigio internacional de la competición y, por ello, no consideran aceptable que se cree una nueva liga en Europa sin que los jugadores participen también económicamente. Se avecinan problemas serios para la NBA Europa pues de todos es sabido lo combativo que es el sindicato de jugadores, un colectivo siempre durísimo de roer para la NBA y sus propietarios. El nuevo director ejecutivo del sindicato de jugadores considera que NBA Europa se está construyendo sobre el valor generado por los jugadores de la NBA. En la entrevista con el prestigioso medio estadounidense afirma que existe una situación muy delicada que les afecta gravemente porque se está creando una competición rival en la que los jugadores no participan ni deportiva ni económicamente. “Tenemos un problema muy serio con eso”, asegura. El argumento jurídico y económico de Kelly se apoya en que NBA Europa generará ingresos relacionados con el baloncesto. Por tanto, aunque no reclama que los jugadores reciban el mismo 51% de los ingresos que actualmente perciben de la NBA -el denominado BRI (Business Related Income) que establece que deben cobrar su parte de todo lo que NBA haga usando el logo de la NBA-, sí considera que debe existir una participación económica. Kelly habla de una cantidad negociada “de buena fe”. El actual convenio colectivo, que expira el 30 de junio de 2030, aunque cualquiera de las partes puede comunicar en octubre de 2028 su intención de rescindirlo anticipadamente, no obliga a la NBA a compartir con los jugadores los ingresos de la futura competición europea, pero la NBPA quiere cambiar esa situación en la próxima negociación del CBA. Kelly aclara que todavía no existen negociaciones formales con la NBA ni con Adam Silver. De momento, explica, son conversaciones preliminares en las que el sindicato está exponiendo sus preocupaciones, pero advierte que cuando llegue la negociación propiamente dicha la NBPA será firme en las cuestiones que considera fundamentales. Y la de percibir su parte del negocio de la NBA Europa será una de ellas. Vienen curvas para ese proyecto antes incluso de tomar forma.

articles.title: Sue Bird claims WNBA players wanted to 'shut up and dribble' despite leading 2020 political push
articles.summary: Sue Bird now claims WNBA players wanted to "shut up and dribble" in 2020, but her own words from that era openly contradict her revisionist stance.
articles.body: "We would have loved to shut up and dribble." That's what Sue Bird said on a recent episode of her podcast. Yes, Sue Bird. The same woman who was engaged to Megan Rapinoe for more than five years before they announced their split earlier this year now claims that she wanted to "shut up and dribble" instead of diving headfirst into progressive politics in 2020. Bird said the players "would have loved to shut up and dribble because that meant we were talking about basketball." But the "intersectionality of it all," she argued, meant they "kind of had to speak on these things." My goodness. I'm not sure a more ridiculous piece of revisionist history has ever been uttered into a microphone. WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT Bird was a WNBPA vice president in 2020. That was the season that the WNBA put Black Lives Matter on its courts, launched the Justice Movement and created a Social Justice Council. The league and its players repeatedly spoke out on progressive political topics like voting rights, LGBTQ advocacy and gun control. This wasn’t just a handful of players sounding off online, either. The league and union built it into the fabric of the season. Players even went so far as to openly support a Democrat candidate for U.S. Senate by wearing shirts that said "Vote Warnock" prior to games. Bird now wants people to believe they were forced to do all those things. Here's the problem: Bird's new stance is openly contradicted by... Bird's old stance. Bird’s 2020 words contradict her 2026 comments "Our season was going to have to be played with social justice messages, on our jerseys, on the floor, forefront." That’s what Sue Bird said in an October 2020 interview with NPR. Quite a bit different than "we would have loved to shut up and dribble," huh? Bird didn’t just say she wanted social justice at the forefront of the WNBA’s 2020 season. She called it nonnegotiable for the players. And Bird said the league was on board "right from the jump." THE LEFT WANTS CAITLIN CLARK, SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM TO SHUT UP AND DRIBBLE WHEN IT COMES TO TRANS SPORTS Then the WNBA got even more explicit. Players wore "Vote Warnock" shirts in support of Democrat Raphael Warnock during his Senate race against then-Atlanta Dream co-owner Kelly Loeffler. Loeffler had criticized the WNBA for dedicating its season to Black Lives Matter, and the players’ union had already called for her ouster. Bird had a different idea: go after her Senate seat. Axios reported the idea to publicly support Warnock came directly from Bird. "What a great way for us to get the word out about this man, and hopefully put him in the Senate," Bird said at the time. In 2020, Bird was openly thinking about how WNBA players could help put a Democrat in the U.S. Senate. In 2026, though, Bird says the WNBA has become a "lightning rod" for political fights the league office cannot be expected to solve. She brought up Donald Trump and wondered whether anyone, including Democrats, had figured out how not to be manipulated by the way he operates. How, Bird asked, was the WNBA supposed to figure that out "overnight"? She said the league office might be getting too much flak for failing to handle things that even politicians paid to handle them cannot figure out. STEPHEN A. SMITH BLAMES ‘THE RIGHT’ FOR WNBA FIRESTORM, SAYS LEAGUE ‘LEFT THE DOOR OPEN’ The through-line for all of Bird's commentary was remarkably consistent, although misguided. Her central claim was that the WNBA and its players were innocent victims and unwilling players in a political game in 2020 and they are, once again, going through the same problem. But Bird’s guest on that episode, ESPN reporter Ramona Shelburne, correctly noted that's not exactly true. Shelburne called the WNBA "a more willing participant" in political conversations because its players are willing to weigh in on hot-button issues. She said the WNBA sits in the middle of the culture wars, but players, coaches, front offices and the league all have a choice about whether to engage. "Right now the choice seems to have been that you are engaging," Shelburne said. Exactly. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In 2020, Bird called social-justice messaging nonnegotiable. And when players fought with Kelly Loeffler, she helped turn it into a campaign for Raphael Warnock. Bird clearly knows the difference. She's choosing revisionist history anyway.

articles.title: College Basketball In Crosshairs of Pro-Athlete NCAA Eligibility Chaos
articles.summary: The Big 12, SEC, and ACC have extended bans to include basketball.
articles.body:
For the first time in college sports, top conferences have now implemented different rules about which athletes are eligible to play on their teams.

Following a bombshell ruling allowing several players who signed NFL contracts to return to college, the Big Ten adopted bans on professional football players returning to college. The Big SEC and ACC chose to put in place a similar ban for football—but also added basketball to the list. The Big 12 implemented a policy for all sports.

Even more than football, basketball will feel the biggest impact of these new policies. In some cases, they ban players who may have gotten eligibility under NCAA rules. In others, they've caused confusion about the complex international professional basketball rules less relevant in football. And looming over it all is the flood of lawsuits and court decisions.

"I think everyone believes things have got to change," one power conference administrator told Front Office Sports. "But I think until things do change, everyone goes week by week with this. Like, 'What's gonna happen this week?'"

In men's college basketball, the eligibility landscape has already been marred with confusion for the past two years, from the NCAA allowing some players to return from the G League but banning others who have signed NBA contracts, including two-way deals. The NCAA has faced challenges to those rules, however, as in the case of Charles Bediako , who sued to return to Alabama after a stint in the G League that included an NBA two-way contract. It was able to fight off that particular challenge.

The chaos was only amplified this summer in the wake of the NCAA's "age-based" eligibility policy , granting athletes five years to play five seasons, up from four. Players nationwide who started college in 2022 but exhausted four seasons of eligibility filed lawsuits to force the NCAA to include them in that policy. (One of those cases included NFL players—two of whom, Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, signed deals to return to LSU .)

Now, for Big 12, ACC, and SEC players, conference-level restrictions add to the sport's murky eligibility landscape. As of Thursday afternoon, these were the only conferences that have publicly announced policies applying to basketball professional experience.

First, the leagues ban players who entered the NBA or WNBA drafts but did not properly withdraw. In men's basketball, underclassmen can declare for the draft, but must decide to opt out if they want to return to school.

Players are automatically entered once they exhausted their college eligibility, however; the SEC policy allows players from the 2022 freshman class whose names were automatically entered into the draft, and who have now won an injunction for a fifth year, to return. (For women's basketball, players must be four years removed from high school graduation or 22 years old—meaning most won't enter the draft before exhausting their college eligibility anyway.)

They also bar the return of players who have signed NBA and WNBA contracts, or who have appeared on these rosters. But they take a stricter stance than NCAA rules: Men's players can't have participated in the G League, either. The Big 12 bans players who signed any "professional league" contract, while the SEC specifically stipulates G League and NBA contracts. The ACC's policy notes that NBA Summer League contracts mean Exhibit 10, two-way, or "any agreement providing for compensation beyond expenses and per diem."

And then there's the question of international players—teams are increasingly more likely to recruit athletes who played professionally overseas. The Big 12 has barred all professional leagues—but will make an exception for international athletes who played in the pros overseas before coming to college in the first place. Players can't, however, leave college and go pro overseas and then come back.

What's more, the patchwork of conference rules has created an uneven set of rules. For example, players who left college and signed G League contracts can't return to play men's college basketball in the SEC, Big 12, and ACC; but they could return to other leagues that haven't yet passed a similar rule.

However, other leagues are rushing to follow the lead of these conferences: The Big East was set to meet Thursday to discuss basketball options, FOS confirmed.

Multiple sources across conferences said they supported the decision for leagues to levy specific rules preventing professional participation. One source associated with a power conference school described it as a feeling of "relief;" the administrator said it provided a sense of "optimism."

But that doesn't mean there won't be complications with enforcement. For example, it could be hard to police the question about whether players have signed contracts, given that it's often difficult to determine whether players have actually put pen to paper on G League, Exhibit 10, or other deals versus agreeing to them verbally.

Then, there's also whether the league-wide rules will hold up in court. The problem: If courts prohibit the NCAA from enforcing specific eligibility rules, could these rulings also, by proxy, apply to conferences?

That's the argument being made in multiple cases right now, including that of Kentucky transfer Mark Mitchell, whose attorneys filed an amended complaint Thursday arguing the SEC can't enforce eligibility rules enjoined by a court order stopping the NCAA.

Sources say they are all waiting to see how the league will respond to LSU rostering its football players as well as monitoring the case of former St. John's standout RJ Luis Jr., who won an injunction to play at LSU this season despite going through the NBA Draft process and signing with multiple NBA teams.

In addition to asking the court to clarify that the injunction applies to the SEC as well as the NCAA, LSU itself could sue the SEC once it receives a penalty. Or, the SEC could sue LSU in advance to get a judge to establish it can legally enforce conference penalties against the school (like the Big 12 did in the case of Brendan Sorsby ).

"I think there's a chance that each of the four Power 4 conferences have their 'Sorsby' moments," the power conference administrator said. "But I certainly think everyone's looking to see how the SEC navigates, executes, and implements this."

articles.title: Kevin Durant Could Earn Massive Payout from Early Hugging Face Investment After Reported $12.9B Sale
articles.summary: Kevin Durant is one of the greatest basketball players in history and, apparently, a fairly shrewd investor as well.
articles.body:
Kevin Durant is one of the greatest basketball players in history and, apparently, a fairly shrewd investor as well.

Insider Joe Pompliano reported Thursday that Durant and his business partner, Rich Kleiman, invested $100,000 in the seed round and $150,000 in the Series A round of fundraising for the company Hugging Face.

That is notable as Nvidia has reportedly acquired Hugging Face for $12.9 billion.

"He likely made more than $60 million in this investment alone," Pompliano wrote. "That is one of the best athlete investments ever."

The total payout is not confirmed since Durant's share of the company is not public, but the NBA star will clearly benefit from getting in early on a rising company.

Durant posted about his investment on social media in 2017:

April Roach and Kai Nicol-Schwarz of CNBC reported on the acquisition Thursday and noted "if completed, the acquisition would put one of the most widely used platforms for sharing and working with open-source AI models under Nvidia's ownership, expanding the chipmaker's reach further into the software and model ecosystem."

As for Durant, he is set to make $43.9 million this season for the Houston Rockets before a 2027-28 player option of $46.1 million, per Spotrac .

He has also earned $501.1 million in career earnings during his NBA tenure.

It's safe to say Durant, who will turn 38 years old next month, is set up well for retirement thanks to his basketball earnings and investment.

That is notable since he revealed during an episode of Boardroom Talks (11:40 mark) retirement is on his mind after former teammate Russell Westbrook called it a career.

"I'm on deck," he said . "… It's a young man's game. Even though I still feel like I can play, I always hear, 'you're 38, you're 39. You're getting up there.' I get that. But I put everything into the game, and I'm cool with whatever happens moving forward. I'm going to continue putting everything into the game until I can't."

When retirement does come, perhaps he can look further into investments like the one he made with Hugging Face.

articles.title: ‘Natural-Born Hater’ — NBA World Claps Back As Stephen Jackson Kicks LeBron James Out of Michael Jordan Tier After Joining ‘Championship-Ready’ 76ers
articles.summary: Most believed LeBron James was slated to join either the Miami Heat or the Cleveland Cavaliers this summer. So, it was quite the shock when the 22-time NBA A...
articles.body:
Most believed LeBron James was slated to join either the Miami Heat or the Cleveland Cavaliers this summer. So, it was quite the shock when the 22-time NBA All-Star signed a two-year, $7.9 million veteran minimum contract with the Philadelphia 76ers.

Stephen Jackson has since gotten over the shock and relegated James to a lower tier of "NBA GOATs" because of the move, citing ring-chasing as the reason for the shift in his all-time rankings. That led the NBA world to bombard Jackson with takes defending James.

Stephen Jackson's Hot Take Prompts NBA Fans To Defend LeBron James

Jackson took to his "All The Smoke" podcast to speak on why he believes James dropped from the top tier of all-time player rankings after his move to Philadelphia.

"All the talk you hear about the GOATs and comparing him to [Michael] Jordan and Kobe [Bryant]. For me, Cleveland is the only thing that made sense for me to keep him in that conversation," Jackson said .

"Going to a team that's already championship-ready. That's not what I would look at as the best player in the league challenging himself. I don't think that was a 'best player in the league' move."

The NBA world did not take too kindly to this stance from "Stack Jack."

"I never heard someone say go to a worse team so you can 'challenge yourself,' HE'S 41," one basketball fan pushed back .

Onyx Odds pointed out that James will be 42 this December and will be in the NBA competing for a title, while Jordan, at 42, had already been retired for years. The caption read, "LeBron at 42 vs. Michael Jordan at 42."

Another account called out Jackson for hating, saying, "Y'all were saying Jaylen Brown was overrated and Joel Embiid is cooked. Now this is a championship-ready team? Natural-born haters."

One 76ers fan defended James, saying , "You're right, he's in a league of his own above them."

Multiple fans also pointed out how the 76ers were a seventh seed last season and in the play-in tournament after finishing with a middling 45-37 record.

"That team was not championship-ready. And LeBron has been passed Kobe a very long time ago, so I don't get the obsession with bringing him up," one fan said .

Another kept it simple, adding , "They were just a 7 seed what the [expletive] are we talking about?"

The Cavaliers were also a higher seed than the 76ers last season, posting a 52-30 record as the fourth seed. They also feature All-Star talent such as Donovan Mitchell, James Harden, and Evan Mobley.

So, the four-time MVP signing with the Cavaliers, aside from the homecoming narrative, could have technically been met with the same amount of vitriol as his joining the 76ers.

James hasn't been shy about admitting that, at this point in his career, his main goal is to compete for his fifth championship. He authored a statement after the decision, writing:

"I'm not going for money. I'm not going for family. What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning another championship. I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team."

So, in his own way, James has also admitted to ring-chasing, and unabashedly so.
